newsitem.title: UK: British para to get new appeal in Belfast murder.
newsitem.headline: British para to get new appeal in Belfast murder.

text.p: The government granted leave on Thursday for appeal judges to re-examine the conviction of a British soldier who was sentenced for murdering a teenage Catholic girl in Northern Ireland but freed after only two years in jail.
The release of paratrooper Lee Clegg in 1995 sparked riots in Catholic areas by young people who said it showed the legal system was biased against them.

But his cause is backed by establishment figures and retired officers who argue that he was harshly treated for a hair-trigger reaction in the throes of a guerrilla war against the Irish Republican Army.
Britain said on Thursday that new evidence had come to light that merited Clegg's case being sent to the Appeal Court.

"In the light of new forensic evidence submitted to me by his solicitors I have decided to use my power under the Criminal Appeal (Northern Ireland) Act 1980 to refer the case of Lee William Clegg to the Court of Appeal," Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew said in a statement.
He did not say what the new evidence was.
Karen Reilly, 17, was shot dead when Clegg opened fire on a car in which she was a passenger as it sped past an army patrol on a dark road in mostly Catholic west Belfast in 1990.
BBC radio quoted her father Sean as saying he was "deeply hurt and bitter about the decision to re-examine Clegg's conviction, but not surprised."

Catholic nationalist politician Alex Attwood was caustic. "This case stinks...because a man who was convicted of murder was released from prison in a differential way from all those others who have been convicted of murder," he told BBC radio.
"It may yet stink again when this case is heard in the Court of Appeal."
Clegg was convicted in June 1993 and appealed to the Court of Appeal and to Britain's highest court, the House of Lords, but the judges turned him down.
Last July his lawyers made a submission to refer the case back again to the Appeal Court.

Catholic nationalists who are opposed to Britain's rule over Northern Ireland saw his early release on license as evidence of discrimination against them. Guerrilla and civilian murderers normally serve at least 10 years in prison.
His release, which came during a 17-month IRA truce abandoned last February, caused some of the most serious rioting for many years in Catholic zones.
Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, described the decision as an insult to Reilly's family.
"The decision once again highlights the manner in which the British government legitimises and protects members of the Crown forces who kill Irish civilians," he said.
The decision comes at a time of increased tension in the province with IRA guerrillas stepping up activities and fears that the province could slide back into sectarian warfare.
